clue.text: Basque infiltrator holding shilling interest with VAT transaction?

indicators.note: holding says the rearranged letters wrap round and contain the shilling's letter
a transaction here is read as a working-over, so the letters of interest and VAT are dealt into a new order

parts.note: taken as written: value added tax
S is the old abbreviation for a shilling, a pre-decimal British coin

explanation.surface: A Basque separatist agent squabbles over shillings of interest on a tax deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Basque' looks like the Spanish region, but it is the corset-like garment; 'transaction' makes TRANVESTITE, which 'holding' wraps round S.
explanation.definitionFit: A man who wears a basque, a women's undergarment, is crossdressing, slipping into it in the playful sense of an infiltrator.

clue.text: Champion wife's held in the air

indicators.note: held in says one piece sits inside the other, the wife's piece within the air

parts.note: an air is a tune or melody
Eve was made from Adam's rib, so a rib stands for a wife in crosswords; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A champion's wife is lifted aloft in celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the air' looks like hoisted up, but 'held in' is the container and 'the air' is a TUNE.
explanation.definitionFit: A tribune was a Roman official who defended the plebs, so the word means a champion or defender of the people.

clue.text: Waste something won by top team

definitions.meaning: to waste away, wither from disuse
read as two words, a prize cup awarded to the winners

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the answer as A TROPHY, the cup the best side carries off.
explanation.definitionFit: To waste away is to wither, shrink from disuse; the second sense is a cup or prize.

clue.text: Work European hours without an Incredible Hulk?

indicators.note: work is taken as a verb, to work over or knead the letters into a new order
without here means lacking, so the letters of the clue's 'an' are taken away from the word European

parts.note: HRS is the standard abbreviation for hours

explanation.surface: A complaint about European working time rules, offered without the green giant to help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without an' removes AN from EUROPEAN, leaving EUROPE; 'Work' then rearranges EUROPE plus HRS.
explanation.definitionFit: The Incredible Hulk is a Marvel comic-book strongman, an example of a costumed crimefighter with special powers.

clue.text: Getting a hiding, can one call the shots too rashly here?

indicators.note: hiding says the rearranged letters conceal the clue's 'a' somewhere within them
doing something too rashly is doing it wildly, so the words can one call the shots are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A gunslinger who takes too many risks ends up getting beaten in a Wild West bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting' is a link: the jumbled CANONECALLTHESHOTS gets A hidden inside it. The whole clue paints the answer, a semi-&lit where 'here' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The final saloon reached is the place of a last opportunity, where anyone gambling recklessly will finally be beaten.

clue.text: Is this treatment working?

parts.note: read as asking whether a treatment is effective, but really describing a treatment built around work: rehabilitation through everyday jobs and activities

explanation.surface: A patient anxiously wonders whether the therapy is having any effect.
explanation.definitionFit: This rehabilitation helps people recover the skills of daily living and work through practical activity, so it is treatment by working.

clue.text: Companion I repeatedly take in the air to inspirit

parts.note: CH is the abbreviation for Companion of Honour, a British order

indicators.note: repeatedly says the take letter is used twice in succession

parts.note: R, from the Latin recipe on prescriptions, means take
up means aloft, in the air

explanation.surface: A friend and I keep breathing the fresh air to raise our spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Companion' looks like a person, but it is CH, the Companion of Honour; 'take' is the prescription R.
explanation.definitionFit: To chirrup someone is an old sense of encourage or cheer, as one urges on a horse with chirping sounds.

clue.text: Funny couple putting up new composer

indicators.note: putting up means giving lodging to, so the jumbled letters take in the new letter
funny means odd or peculiar, so the letters of couple are rearranged

explanation.surface: An eccentric pair host a newcomer who writes music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Funny' rearranges COUPLE into POULEC, which 'putting up' wraps round N.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Poulenc was a French twentieth-century writer of music, a member of Les Six.

clue.text: See 6
He dishonestly takes penny Shylock's holding

indicators.note: holding says the moneylender's letters grip the penny's letter inside them

parts.note: Shylock in The Merchant of Venice is a lender at extortionate interest; the 's is 'is'
P is the abbreviation for a penny in British money

explanation.surface: A grasping moneylender pockets a coin by sharp practice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shylock's' reads as possessive, but it is Shylock is, the moneylender USURER.
explanation.definitionFit: A pretender who wrongfully seizes a throne or office is taking something by illegitimate means.

clue.text: One slicing pears up with a plant

indicators.note: slicing says the one figure cuts into the middle of the rearranged letters
up here means in disorder, so the letters of pears are mixed

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone cutting up fruit beside a houseplant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' rearranges PEARS into SPRAE, which I slices into as SP-I-RAE; A follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiraea is a genus of flowering shrubs in the rose family, such as meadowsweet.

clue.text: Imitation Indy, say, with no front page story ultimately

indicators.note: with no front says the page letter is removed from the start of the newspaper

parts.note: the Indy is the nickname of The Independent, an example of a newspaper

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word story

explanation.surface: A copycat edition of The Independent runs without its front-page lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'front page' looks like the newspaper's cover, but 'with no front' strips P (page) from PAPER.
explanation.definitionFit: Aping someone is copying them, so the noun means mimicry.

clue.text: Puzzling, uncannily ace timing

indicators.note: uncannily means strangely, so the letters of ace timing are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone has a mysteriously perfect sense of timing.
explanation.definitionFit: Something mysterious or baffling is hard to work out.

clue.text: I'm Bill, nearly glugging vermouth, which is unwise

parts.note: taken as written, less the apostrophe

indicators.note: glugging means drinking down, so the shortened police letters swallow the vermouth
nearly says the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: the Old Bill is British slang for the police
IT is short for Italian vermouth, as in gin and it

explanation.surface: A man named Bill admits to knocking back vermouth, which is foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a name, but it is the police (the Old Bill); 'nearly' leaves POLIC, and 'glugging' puts IT inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Impolitic action is injudicious, showing poor judgment rather than prudence.

clue.text: Having problems pouring pint in free house? Just the opposite

indicators.note: just the opposite reverses the stated container, so the house letters go inside the pint letters instead
pouring means sloshing out, so the letters of pint are jumbled
free means loosed, so the letters of house are rearranged

explanation.surface: A drinker sloshes a pint in a pub not tied to a brewery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pouring' makes INTP and 'free' makes HESOU. The clue says the pint goes in the house; 'Just the opposite' puts the house inside. A free house is a British pub not tied to one brewery.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in trouble or difficulty is an idiom meaning to be facing problems.

clue.text: See 7
Hard-to catch murderer nearly arrested over in E2

indicators.note: arrested means held, so the pair of letters detains the reversed killer between them

parts.note: E2 is E squared, the letter E twice; it is also an East London postcode

indicators.note: over says the shortened murderer letters are turned backwards
nearly drops the last letter of the word

parts.note: a murderer is a killer

explanation.surface: A slippery murderer is finally caught in East London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'E2' looks like the East London postcode, but it is E squared; 'nearly' leaves KILLE and 'over' turns it round, then 'arrested' holds that between the two Es.
explanation.definitionFit: Being slippery as an eel, wriggling free, is hard to grab hold of.

clue.text: Sing introductions to Get Ready and Somethin Stupid

indicators.note: introductions to points to the opening letter of each following word

explanation.surface: A list of hit songs to perform: Get Ready and Somethin' Stupid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sing' looks like a request to perform; it is the slang sense, to inform. Get Ready and Somethin' Stupid are 1960s pop songs.
explanation.definitionFit: In criminal slang, to sing is to inform to the police, the same as to grass, a British word for informing.

clue.text: High tar cigs affecting insides

indicators.note: high means intoxicated, so the letters of tar cigs are muddled

explanation.surface: High-tar cigarettes damage your internal organs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High' looks like it describes the tar level, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something to do with the stomach concerns the internal organs.

clue.text: When non-flier enters, help the idiot!

indicators.note: enters says the flightless bird goes into the help word

parts.note: aid means help
the rhea is a large flightless South American bird

explanation.surface: Someone panics when a passenger afraid to fly comes on board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'non-flier' suggests a nervous traveller, but it is the RHEA, a bird that cannot fly.
explanation.definitionFit: A scatterbrained, empty-headed person is a fool.

clue.text: Gets to the chalk stacks

definitions.meaning: a row of chalk pinnacles off the western tip of the Isle of Wight, in southern England

explanation.surface: Someone climbs right up to the pillars of chalk.
explanation.definitionFit: To annoy someone is to provoke them persistently; the second sense names famous sea stacks with a lighthouse.

clue.text: Do I know if I do this?

definitions.text: Do I know if I do this?

parts.words: Do I know if I do this?
parts.note: the gesture of raising the shoulders means 'I don't know', so doing it answers the question with a pun

explanation.surface: A puzzled person asks whether a gesture signals knowledge.
explanation.definitionFit: Lifting the shoulders is the body-language sign for ignorance or indifference.

clue.text: After sin, initially religious one's left pure every five years

parts.note: lust is one of the seven deadly sins

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the word religious

parts.note: A means one; the 's is 'has', a link

explanation.surface: After sinning, a devout person ends up purified at five-year intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' is a link: the pieces already follow in order. The Roman lustrum was a purification held every five years.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective relates to ritual purification, and in Rome to the lustrum, the cleansing ceremony each five-year census period.

clue.text: I'm disgusted, interrupting play — it's more like spring than winter!

indicators.note: interrupting says the exclamation breaks into the middle of the play

parts.note: King Lear is a Shakespeare play
fie is an old exclamation of disgust

explanation.surface: An offended theatregoer breaks into a performance, which is livelier than a winter's tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm disgusted' is a phrase giving FIE, which breaks into LEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Trees have more foliage in spring than in winter, when branches are bare.

clue.text: Wreck plans for right exercises in list for organiser

indicators.note: in says the right-plus-exercises letters go inside the list

parts.note: a to-do list is what an organiser keeps
PE is physical education, exercises at school

explanation.surface: An organiser keeps a list of fitness sessions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wreck plans for' is the definition: to scupper a scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: To sink or scupper a scheme is to ruin it, as a missile sinks a ship.

clue.text: Gay cleric's forged passport in compound

indicators.note: forged means faked, so the letters of gay cleric's are reworked

parts.note: a passport is ID, identification

explanation.surface: A gay clergyman's fake travel document is discovered in a compound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forged' makes LYSERGICAC; 'in' is a link joining the wordplay to the definition, though it reads as an insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: LSD is a chemical substance, a hallucinogenic drug derived from ergot.
